questions.q: What does the Slow Request Log from Lesson 1 NOT tell you on its own, that script-level debugging adds?
options: Whether the transaction happened at all
The URL of the page that was slow
Exactly which individual script or method consumed the time within a slow transaction
The name of the user who triggered the transaction
questions.explain: The Slow Request Log gives you a total and a rough category; script-level debugging breaks that total down script by script, down to a specific Script Include method.

questions.q:
A debug panel for one incident save reads:
*** Script: Business Rule "Validate Priority" (incident) - 142 ms
*** Script: Business Rule "Update Related Problem" (incident) - 1894 ms
***   Script Include: "IncidentUtils.syncRelatedProblems" - 1820 ms
*** Script: Client Script "Set mandatory fields" (incident) - 8 ms
Which script is responsible for the overwhelming majority of the transaction's time?
options: Set mandatory fields, the client script
Validate Priority, the first business rule to run
All four scripts contribute roughly equally
The IncidentUtils.syncRelatedProblems method, nested inside Update Related Problem
questions.explain: 1820 of the business rule's 1894 ms, and nearly all of the transaction's ~2044 ms total, is inside that one Script Include method.

questions.q: How do you turn on script-level debugging for a transaction?
options: Open the Developer menu from the profile picture, enable developer mode, switch on toggles like Debug Business Rule and Debug Script, then reproduce the exact transaction
Open the system log and filter by the word "slow"
Raise the response-time threshold on the Slow Request Log
Ask a user to describe how slow the page felt
questions.explain: Debug toggles live under the Developer menu; once enabled, reproducing the exact slow transaction populates the debug panel at the bottom of the page.

questions.q: In that same debug panel, what does the indented line '***   Script Include: "IncidentUtils.syncRelatedProblems" - 1820 ms' indicate?
options: A completely separate, unrelated transaction that happened to log at the same time
Time spent inside a Script Include method that the business rule above it called, counted as part of that business rule's own total
The total time spent on database indexing for the whole instance
An error that occurred while the business rule was running
questions.explain: The nesting shows the method is called from within the business rule listed above it, and its time is part of that business rule's 1894 ms.

questions.q: Why is picking which business rule to investigate first based on its name or how complex it looks a bad strategy?
options: Because ServiceNow randomizes business rule execution order on every save
Because business rule names are hidden from developers by default
Because debugging tools can only be turned on once per instance
Because a script's name or apparent complexity has no reliable relationship to its actual execution time — only measurement does
questions.explain: A simple-looking rule can hide a slow Script Include call, and a complex-looking one can run in milliseconds — the debug panel measures instead of guessing.
